children: By Gavin Maguire

A record-strong El Nino weather pattern this winter bodes well for wind power generation potential across Europe, and could help limit the amount of gas required by utilities over Europe's peak heating demand period.

Although El Nino is measured by sea temperatures in the central Pacific Ocean, its influence extends across much of the planet and can drive stronger winds and above-normal winter temperatures in Europe.

For European utilities, the potential combination of more sustained winds alongside warmer-than-usual weather through early 2027 means the region's natural gas needs may remain constrained this winter.
This could render moot worries about Europe's below-normal gas inventories, and may dash hopes for a late-year swell in LNG imports by European traders.
SUPERSIZED EL NINO UNDERWAY

El Nino is a periodic warming of sea ​surface temperatures in the Eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. It occurs every two to seven years and tends to ​last up to 12 months, and can impact rainfall and temperature patterns in every region.

children: This year's El Nino "may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began. So ⁠literally off the charts," World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said at a Geneva press conference earlier this month.
Recent record-setting heat waves and droughts in Europe have already been linked to this year's El Nino, but the system may not be done impacting the region's weather patterns.

Indeed, the peak in El Nino readings is not expected to emerge until sometime between November and January, according to meteorological data service Nebbo, which means that Europe's winter weather trends will also be affected.

"El Nino winters tend to drive a negative pressure anomaly over the central North Atlantic. This steers the jet stream, channelling westerlies more directly into the UK, the North Sea, Ireland, and Scandinavia," Nebbo's Head of Technology, Gerard Castro, wrote in a recent report.
FAVOURABLE WINDS

If these weather patterns unfold as expected, the wind farms off the North Sea and across Germany, the United Kingdom and France — home to a majority of Europe's total wind capacity — should see a sustained uptick in generation later in 2026.

This would be a welcome change from the sub-par wind output trends seen in recent years caused by prolonged spells of below-normal wind speeds at turbine level, which forced Europe's utilities to dial up generation from other sources.

These weak wind bouts were particularly evident in Germany, Europe's top wind power producer, where the term Dunkelflaute was coined to describe periods of dark doldrums when little solar or wind power was generated.
The peaks in German wind electricity production in 2024, 2025 and so far in 2026 came far below previous calendar year peaks due to a lack of sustained breezes in dense wind farm corridors.
And these wind generation shortfalls came despite steady increases to Germany's total wind farm capacity, which has climbed to a record of around 82 gigawatts as of mid-2026, according to Ember.

However, there are signs that Germany's wind generation trends are beginning to turn around, with output during August coming in more than 30% above the average for that month during the prior two years, according to generation data from LSEG.

Germany's wind farms generated around 390,189 megawatt hours of electricity per hour (MWh/h) in August, compared to around 298,000 MWh/h during August of last year and 277,075 MWh/h during August of 2024.
GAS SQUEEZE
If wind speeds pick up as expected as autumn sets in, generation levels from Germany's wind farms should continue to press higher, resulting in system-wide repercussions for utilities.
Wind farms are the single largest source of electricity in Germany, accounting for around 28% of total utility-supplied electricity, according to Ember.
Coal is the next largest electricity source (around 20%), while natural gas is the third largest with a roughly 16% annual generation share.
At the system level, higher wind power generation tends to result in cuts to both coal and gas-fired production in Germany and across Northern Europe more broadly.

However, with benchmark European natural gas prices currently holding near their highest since late 2022, it is likely that utilities will attempt to pare their gas burn more quickly than coal during periods of high wind output.

Any prolonged stretches of reduced gas burns in Germany and elsewhere should limit any drawdowns in regional gas inventories, and may also limit buying interest for fresh gas supplies in the form of liquefied natural gas imports.
GETTING WARMER
In addition to generating breezier conditions across Europe's largest wind belts, strong El Ninos have historically also resulted in milder average temperatures over the winter months.
Strong El Ninos have tended to favour what is known as a positive North Atlantic Oscillation, which is where high pressure brings in mild, wet air over mainland Europe.
And LSEG's weather forecasters are currently calling for those conditions to prevail into 2027.

"Temperatures are likely to be warmer across continental Europe and the Black Sea Region, with cold risks limited to Scandinavia and north/central Russia," LSEG weather analysts recently posted in an outlook for the 2026-27 winter.
Of course forecasts change, and the projections for a synchronous strengthening in El Nino measurements could peter out and yield a drier and colder winter than is currently expected.

But for now most major forecasters foresee a mild and breezy winter ahead for Europe, which could lift wind farm generation far above recent stunted levels and trigger sustained cuts to gas consumption across the region.
